title: Satyakama tells the truth
hookLine: asked his family line, the boy tells the plain truth about his mother, and the teacher accepts him for it (Chandogya Upanishad 4.4)

lines: A FORM YOU'D RATHER NOT FILL.
cards: Father's name. Previous address. Reason for leaving your last job.
Forms ask questions like these, and there's often a small pull to round the answer off, to make it tidier than a life actually was.
Now suppose the question is asked out loud, by a teacher a boy badly wants to study with, and the honest answer is: I don't know who my father is.
That's where a boy named Satyakama found himself, in an old Indian text called the Chandogya Upanishad.

teach.b: The Chandogya is one of the Upanishads, the philosophical texts that close the Vedas. Satyakama wants to become a student of the sacred teaching.
In that world, a teacher would ask a new student his family line, his gotra. So Satyakama asks his mother, Jabala, and she tells him the truth.
When I was young, she says, I moved around a great deal, working as a servant, and that's when I had you. I don't know your family line. My name is Jabala.
Your name is Satyakama. Call yourself Satyakama Jabala. No cover story.
The boy goes to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, who asks: what is your family line? Satyakama repeats his mother's words, exactly.

And the teacher says, as the Upanishad tells it, that only a true Brahmin could speak like that. Go and fetch firewood, he says: I'll take you as my student, because you have not turned away from the truth.
His name joins satya, truth, and kama, desire: one who loves truth. It suits him.
People take the teacher's answer in different ways.

teach.h: HE REPEATS IT, WORD FOR WORD.
teach.b: Some hear a radical idea, that truthfulness, not birth, is what makes a person fit to learn.

teach.h: YOU HAVE NOT TURNED FROM TRUTH.
teach.b: Others point out that the story still speaks inside the world of caste, and simply finds its highest mark in a boy's honesty.
Either way, look at the heroes: a mother who didn't lie to her son, and a son who didn't lie for her.

how: Hindu teachers and readers of the Upanishads often tell the story of Satyakama Jabala as a lesson in truthfulness, and it is often discussed in debates about birth, caste and fitness to learn.

o: a sage who hid his low birth to study the Vedas
a teacher who tested students by asking their lineage
a boy who gave the plain truth instead of a family line

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

s: Satyakama invents a family line to be accepted
he repeats his mother's words exactly, and is accepted for it.
his name means something like one who loves truth
all scholars read the story the same way
some hear truthfulness over birth; others note it still speaks inside the world of caste.

games.q: you're Satyakama. the teacher asks your family line, and you don't know it. what do you say?
o: repeat exactly what your mother told you
games.why: he repeats his mother's words exactly. the teacher says he hasn't turned from the truth, and sends him for firewood: he's accepted.

practice: Think of one place where you usually round things off: I'm fine, when you're not, a small exaggeration, a detail you always leave out.
Nothing big; just picture saying the plain version once, kindly, to someone safe, and notice that you're still here. The text doesn't say whether Satyakama was afraid; it says he spoke.

wordCard.voice: Satyakama. The boy with no family line to give, who gave the truth instead, and was taken as a student for it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: satya (truth) + kama (desire): one who loves truth. his name in the Chandogya Upanishad.

carryVoice: Your line: the truth is enough. A plain answer, kindly given, was what opened the door. That's day eighty.
